{{nihongo|'''Iwafune Shrine, Konan'''|天忍穂別神社}} is a [[shinto shrine]] in the [[Engishiki Jinmyōchō]]. It is located in [[Tosa Province]].

=== Enshrined deities ===
{{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Ame-no-Oshihomimi-no-Mikoto}} (あめのおしほみみのみこと) – principal deity

{{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Nigihayahi-no-Mikoto}} (にぎはやひのみこと) – enshrined subsidiary deity; son of Ame-no-Oshihomimi-no-Mikoto.
* Sub-shrine within the precincts: Tanabata Shrine. Tanabatatsume (たなばたつめ) = {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Ame-no-Yorozu-Takuhata-Chijihime}} (あめのよろずたくはたちぢひめ) = {{ill|Takuhadachiji-hime|de|Yorozuhatahime|ja|栲幡千千姫命|ru|Ёродзухататоёакицуси-химэ-но микото|zh|栲幡千千姬命|qid=Q11110848}} (たくはたちぢひめ), the wife of Ame-no-Oshihomimi-no-Mikoto.

=== History ===
* The date of establishment is unknown. It predates the completion of the Engishiki in 927 (Engen 5).
* During the Edo period it was called “Oishifune-no-miya” and “Ishifune Daimyōjin.” A record dated April 15, Genkō 4 (1324) refers to Ishifune Daimyōjin Shrine. In Hōei 2 (1705) it was renamed Amaneoshihowake Shrine. In Meiji 5 it was designated a prefectural shrine. According to legend, Ame-no-Oshihowake-no-Mikoto, father of Nigihayahi-no-Mikoto, descended to this land of Yamakawa in Higashikawa Village and enshrined himself there. Nigihayahi-no-Mikoto, longing for his father deity, flew down riding a natural stone boat measuring eight shaku by three shaku and was enshrined together with him. The legendary stone boat still exists today.
* According to the {{ill|Wamyō Ruijushō|de|Wamyō ruijushō|fa|وامیو رویجوشو|fr|Wamyō ruijushō|it|Wamyō ruijushō|ja|和名類聚抄|ko|화명류취초|ru|Вамё Руйдзюсё|uk|Вамьо Руйдзюсьо|zh|和名類聚抄|qid=Q2702542}}, compiled during the Shōhei era (931–938) under the ritsuryō system, Kagami-chō Yamakawa was recorded as part of Ōshi-go in Kami District, suggesting that the entirety of present-day Kagami-chō was included in Ōshi-go. (Kōchi Prefecture Kami District Jūman Site Excavation Report)<ref>{{Cite web|Japanese book|title=Detailed Search - National Archaeological Site Report Database|url=https://sitereports.nabunken.go.jp/ja/search?all=%E5%8D%81%E4%B8%87%E9%81%BA%E8%B7%A1%E7%99%BA%E6%8E%98%E8%AA%BF%E6%9F%BB%E5%A0%B1%E5%91%8A%E6%9B%B8|website=sitereports.nabunken.go.jp|accessdate=2019-05-10}}</ref>
* In the Qinzan Collection written by {{ill|Tani Jinzan|ja|谷秦山|qid=Q63566583}} (personal name Shigetō) of Tosa Nankaku scholarship, dated Hōei 2 (1705), it states that the shrine lay about two ri north of Yasu Town, in Yamakawa of Higashikawa Village, and Volume 14, “Examination of Shikinaisha in Tosa Province,” records the investigation results when it was a prefectural shrine.
* Two ridge tags remain extant: one inscribed “Oishifune Shrine, 4th year of Shōwa, second month, day unknown (1315), Mononobe no Suechika,” and another inscribed “Oishifune Shrine, second day of the second month, Tenshō 6 (1578), Patron Mononobe no Suenobu Mansuke-jō, Jin’emon-jō.”
* Under the modern shrine ranking system, it was registered as a prefectural shrine in Meiji 5, but was later reclassified as a gōsha.<ref>{{Cite web|Japanese book|title=Kōchi Prefecture Shrine Register|url=http://www.shimanto-chimei.com/地名データブック/高知県神社明細帳/|website=Shimanto Town Place Name Dictionary|accessdate=2019-05-10|language=ja-JP}}</ref>

=== Legends ===
* Explanatory sign by the Kagami Town Board of Education: Long ago, a deity named Nigihayahi-no-Mikoto, said to be a grandchild of Amaterasu Ōmikami, rode upon a stone boat and soared through the sky, arriving at the mountain peak of Sumigasako in Yamakawa. Nigihayahi-no-Mikoto first descended upon a mountain in Kawachi Province, then stayed at the foot of Momoo-yama in Yamato Province, and eventually, longing for his father deity Ame-no-Oshihomimi-no-Mikoto, arrived in Tosa Province. His first descent in Tosa was at Kamiokayama (Noichi) near the lower reaches of the Monobe River. From there he passed through Tomike Village, Nishikawa Village, the hamlet of Nagatani, Funato Pass, Suenobu’s Mizufune, and Funatani in Yamakawa, finally arriving at the present shrine in Sumigasako. The stone at Maikawa is said to bear traces of bugaku performed when the deity rested, and in the hamlet of Nagatani there is an Eboshi Rock where he is said to have hung his eboshi cap. The southern valley of the current shrine is called Kattori, where he removed his crown, while the northern valley is called Tsue-dani, where he placed his spear. Nearby Kubisago is said to be where he placed his necklace. The stone boat on which Nigihayahi-no-Mikoto rode lies behind the shrine precincts and takes the form of a gigantic natural stone shaped like a boat. In addition, many small stone boats donated by sailors are piled nearby. As these numerous small stone boats attest, the deity is known both as a guardian of maritime safety and as a deity protecting against smallpox. From Kazuo Katsurai, “Tosa Legends.”

=== Rituals ===
* Autumn festival on November 15

=== Cultural properties ===
* Historic site
** Amaneoshihowake Shrine (Ishifune Shrine) – designated April 1, 1978 (Shōwa 53).
* Natural monument
** Japanese cypress of Ishifune Shrine – designated July 3, 2019 (Reiwa 1).

=== Other ===
* Nigihayahi-no-Mikoto took as his wife {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Tomiyasubime}} (called Mimakiyahime in the Nihon Shoki), the younger sister of Nagasunehiko, and they had {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Umashimaji-no-Mikoto}}. Umashimaji-no-Mikoto is regarded as the ancestor of the Mononobe no Muraji, Hozumi no Omi, and Uneme no Omi clans. In the area around this shrine are the {{ill|Monobe River|ja|物部川|ru|Монобе (река)|zh|物部川|qid=Q11570692}} and the places {{ill|Yasu, Kōchi|ja|夜須町 (高知県)|ko|야스정 (고치현)|uz|Yasu|qid=Q8049931|lt=Yasu Town}} and {{ill|Umaji, Kōchi|ar|قرية أوماجي|ceb|Umaji Mura|cs|Umadži (Kóči)|es|Umaji (Kōchi)|fa|اوماجی، کوچی|fr|Umaji|id|Umaji, Kōchi|it|Umaji|ja|馬路村|ko|우마지촌|my|အုမဂျိရွာ၊ ခိုးချိ|pl|Umaji|ru|Умадзи|tl|Umaji, Kōchi|tr|Umaji|uk|Умаджі|ur|اوماجی، کوچی|zh|馬路村|qid=Q1206380}}, whose pronunciations resemble “Yasu” and “Umashi.”
* The stone boat said to have been ridden by Nigihayahi-no-Mikoto lies behind the shrine precincts and is a gigantic natural stone shaped like a boat. Nearby, numerous small stone boats donated by sailors are scattered about.
